   t = 13.5 s, where it is running close in to the kerb and the wooden fence outside the
   bar. This is measurable from the van's own geometry: as it recedes, the width of its
   visible yellow left flank stays roughly constant in proportion to the width of its rear
   face, instead of shrinking away as it would if the van were simply driving straight up
   the street — which means it is moving out to the right relative to the camera.

4. **The Focus clears the road.** At about t = 13 s to t = 14 s the Focus completes its
   manoeuvre, pulls off the running lane into the parking row on the left, and its brake
   lights go out. By t = 14.4 s the stretch of cobbles ahead of and to the left of the van
   is plainly empty.

5. **The van straightens back out.** From about t = 14.5 s the van stops leaning to the
   right, comes back towards the middle of the now-empty street, and carries on without
   ever having needed the clearance it made for itself.

At no point anywhere in the sixteen seconds is there any oncoming vehicle coming down the
street towards the van.

## The social norm being followed

Stated explicitly, the van is obeying several linked conventions that together amount to
"make room, and tell people you are doing it":

1. **Keep to your own side of the road.** Slovenia drives on the right, so the right-hand
   half of the carriageway is the van's own side. By swinging over to it, the van claims
   only what is its and leaves the rest of the street free for someone else.

2. **Give a manoeuvring vehicle a wide berth rather than crowding it.** The Focus is
   visibly in the middle of a slow parking manoeuvre — brake lights on, nose swinging
   across to the left. The courteous and expected thing is to hang back to the far side of
   the road and let the other driver get on with it, rather than pushing up close, filling
   the gap they need, or pressuring them to hurry. That is exactly what the van does.

3. **Pass a vehicle that is going left on its right.** Because the Focus is moving across
   to the left of the street, the only correct side on which to get past it is the right.
   Going round it on the left would mean cutting straight across the path it is taking.

4. **Signal your intention before you act on it.** The van flashes its right indicator for
   roughly half a second before it starts to move over, announcing the deviation to the car
   in front and to anyone behind. Warning others before changing your line is itself part
   of the norm here.

In plain terms: **the van is deferring to the other driver.** Rather than sitting on the
Focus's tail or squeezing through the middle, it signals, pulls over to the right-hand edge
of the street, and leaves the other car the space it needs to park.

## What changes to make the action redundant

**The obstruction takes itself out of the way before the van gets there.** Between about
t = 13 s and t = 14 s the Ford Focus finishes crossing the road, settles into the parking
row on the left-hand side, and switches off its brake lights. It is no longer in the
traffic lane at all.

Once that has happened, every reason for the van's swing to the right has disappeared:

- **There is no longer a car to make room for.** The vehicle whose manoeuvre the van was
  accommodating is parked and stationary, off the carriageway.
- **There is nothing coming the other way.** No oncoming vehicle appears in the clip at any
  point, so the left-hand half of the street that the van politely surrendered is space
  that nobody else wants or needs.
- **Nothing else is in the road.** The one pedestrian near the van's route — a man in a
  dark t-shirt and green shorts — is over on the far left by the parked cars and has walked
  past and out of shot well before the van's manoeuvre, so he never enters its path.
- **The street ahead is therefore completely empty across its full width.** The van could
  have driven straight up the middle of it and been in nobody's way whatsoever.

The van's own behaviour is the proof. It reaches its furthest-right position at about
t = 13.5 s, precisely as the Focus is clearing the lane; having got there, it finds it has
the whole street to itself, straightens up and drifts back towards the centre of the road
by about t = 14.5 s. The deviation to the right was a sensible and polite response to the
situation at the moment the driver began it, but the situation resolved itself in the
couple of seconds it took to carry out, so by the time the van was over on the right the
courtesy had nothing left to be a courtesy to.

# Answer

**Setting.** A stationary camera looks along a narrow one-way cobbled street (Ljubljana; cars are parked along both kerbs, all facing away from the camera). A silver Ford Focus (LJ 056-FS) drives past the camera at about 3–5 s and then creeps up the street with its brake lights on the whole time. A pedestrian in a dark T-shirt and green shorts has been standing at the left-hand edge of the roadway, between the parked cars, since about 4 s. At roughly 10–11 s the Ford comes to a near-stop right beside that pedestrian, angled slightly toward the left kerb, i.e. it is waiting / preparing to pull in or turn off to the left. A yellow-and-white Pošta Slovenije Renault Kangoo van (MB 20-EKO) then passes the camera at about 10–11 s and comes up directly behind the Ford.

**What the van does.** From about 11 s to 12.6 s the van slows to a crawl behind the Ford with its brake lights on, holding back in the lane rather than pushing past. Then, from about 12.8 s to 13.8 s, it steers noticeably to the right, swinging over to the far right-hand edge of the roadway so that it runs right alongside the wooden planter boxes and the yellow edge line, and goes past the Ford on the Ford's right. After about 14 s it straightens up and drives on down the right-hand side of the street.

**The social norm being followed.** The van's move to the right is the everyday driving courtesy of giving way to, and making room for, a vehicle ahead that has stopped and is manoeuvring (pulling in to park / turning off to the left) in a street too narrow for comfortable side-by-side passing. Instead of tailgating, sounding the horn or squeezing past close to the Ford, the van driver first waits behind it and then moves as far as possible over to the opposite (right-hand) side of the road, leaving the Ford the whole left half of the street to finish what it is doing, and only passes it on the free side with a wide berth. In other words: "keep clear of the car that is parking/turning, give it space and go round it, don't crowd it."

**What changes to make the manoeuvre redundant.** The situation the van is reacting to resolves itself while the van is still steering over. The pedestrian the Ford had been waiting for steps out of the roadway (from about 11.5 s they walk away to the left, between the parked cars and out of the street). As soon as that happens the Ford moves off again: it rolls forward and to the left, into the gap/parking area at the end of the row of parked cars on the left, and by about 14.4–14.8 s it has disappeared from the carriageway entirely behind the parked cars. So by the time the van has completed its swing to the right and reaches that point, there is no longer anything in the lane to make room for: the Ford is already off the road and the street ahead is completely empty (only the parked cars remain). The van's careful move over to the right-hand edge therefore turns out to have been unnecessary — it could simply have carried straight on down the middle of the street. The vehicle it was yielding space to had already left the roadway on its own.

**Summary.** Norm: yielding/giving way — waiting behind and then pulling over to the far right to leave room for the silver Ford that had stopped and was pulling in / turning off to the left, passing it with a wide berth instead of crowding it. Change: the pedestrian the Ford was waiting for moves out of the way, the Ford completes its manoeuvre and drives off the road to the left, so the lane is fully clear before the van gets there and the van's swerve to the right serves no purpose.
